Peer normalization

framework §4

Each raw metric is scored against the peer group for this industry and size band, so the model reads position relative to comparable businesses rather than the raw figure. Blue bars are better than peers and rose bars worse: more concentration or owner dependence than peers scores above zero and is worse.

Standardization applied to every continuous input

Expected transaction value

framework §8

The reported value is the fitted BIZCOMPS equation: log sale price on earnings, revenue, margin, year and a six-digit industry effect, median-calibrated, then placed inside the measured residual spread by the quality inputs. The turn-by-turn build in the table is the old judgment stack — kept so the direction of each adjustment stays visible, but it does not move the value.

Multiple build and resulting value
Anchoring — what the ask does to the price actually achieved

Probability of closing

framework §5–7

The reported probability is a published base rate times a price-gap penalty, scaled down for a buyer pool thinner than typical — it conditions on deal size, the asking gap and the number of buyers contacted, and has no quality term. Quality reaches it only through the gap: at the same ask relative to model value it does not move, but at the same dollar ask a better business has a smaller gap and closes more often. The contribution chart below is the judgment logistic that this replaced: it is kept because the direction of each variable is defensible and it shows what the model would weigh if the coefficients had ever been estimated. It does not move the number above.

Reported probability — base rate and gap penalty
Nonlinear terms currently active (§7)

Time to close

framework §9

The median and the spread are both fitted. The curve is a log-logistic whose median and shape both come from IBBA’s per-band histograms of months to close (4,533 closed deals over 15 quarters, 2020Q1–2021Q4, 2022Q2–2023Q3 and 2025Q4). It describes deals that closed and says nothing about a listing that never does. Both depend on deal size, never on the ask: larger deals take longer, and deals under $500k are more spread out than larger ones. Because of that wider spread, the share closed after about 18 months can still rise slightly with size between $250k and $707k, by under one point. For an ask above model value the median, and the curve with it, is stretched by a judgment multiplier: overpricing costs time.

Median and shape fitted by size band; the median is stretched above model value (g: the ask’s log gap over value, smoothed near zero)

Buyer universe

framework §10–12, §20

Every buyer archetype is placed by how well it fits this company and the price it would pay: its multiple on this business plus the share of its synergy the seller captures. Size is the chance that buyer engages; brightness is the chance it closes. A buyer’s expected value prices it at no more than the ask ceiling, which caps every realised price.

Buyer-specific value and synergy
Competitive effect of a deeper buyer pool

Sensitivity

framework §13

Partial derivatives computed numerically at this company's current position, for two different questions. Left: what the business supports. The fitted BIZCOMPS equation prices earnings, revenue, margin and sector; the nine quality inputs move value only by placing the business inside the fitted residual spread, so their size is measured but their placement is judgment. The ask and the buyer pool cannot change what a business supports, so they are absent here. Right: what the seller should expect to receive — closing probability times the realised price, the quantity the optimizer maximizes. Every lever reaches it, but through the price gap and the ask ceiling, so the two columns can disagree, and when they do the right-hand one is the one a seller banks. The ask and buyer-pool rows show the step they name rather than a derivative: expected proceeds peak at the best ask and bend at a typical pool, where a symmetric difference would average two different slopes.

What the business supports  ∂V/∂xᵢ

What the seller can expect  ∂E[proceeds]/∂xᵢ

Asking price moves the realised price through anchoring, up to the ask itself, while moving the closing probability the other way. The two pull against each other, which is what gives expected proceeds an interior optimum.

How each row is measured

Value gap and interventions

framework §14–17

Each intervention is re-run through the full model rather than added as a flat premium, so overlapping fixes do not double-count. Cost scales with company size.

Value gap if every value-adding change is made
—
Value gap

ΔValue is the change in what the business supports. ΔE[proceeds], ΔPC and ROI are measured on top of a free reprice to the model-supported range, because at an unchanged ask the ask itself caps the price and the improvement is not collected. ΔPC is not zero by construction: the reprice equalises the price gap, but the closing probability also reads the buyer pool and the deal size. Net days are execution days plus the change in the expected (mean) time to close, the basis of the optimizer’s expected days.

Return on an individual intervention

Budget optimizer

framework §18–19

Exhaustive search over every combination of interventions that fits the budget. The two objectives can disagree — maximizing expected proceeds is not always the same as maximizing the seller's overall outcome.

If you need to sell — maximize expected proceeds
—
If you can walk away — maximize overall outcome

Financing check

SBA SOP 50 10 8.1

Individual buyers often borrow under SBA’s 7(a) program, which lends up to $5.00M, and the lender’s first test is debt service coverage: the cash the business throws off after the new owner’s pay and its capital spending, over the payments on all the acquisition debt. SBA’s rules for a change of ownership, in force for loans numbered from October 1, 2026, set the floor at 1.25× for an initial acquisition and 1.15× for an established business expanding, on the seller’s historical earnings, not projections, and cap all the acquisition debt at the business valuation. When an ask fails, the buyer needs more cash, a larger seller note on full standby, or a lower price.

    Where these parameters come from

    Every number the console produces carries one of three badges. Fitted means a regression was run against observed transaction outcomes and the error is measured. Aggregate means a published summary statistic was read off, so the number is real but can only respond to what the publisher tabulated. Judgment means a person picked it and no data constrains it. These tables are generated from the live model constants, so they cannot drift out of step with what the console actually runs.

    Save each business you value, record what happened when it went to market, and the console compares your deals with its own predictions: what your closed deals sold for against the price it expected, how often your listings closed against the odds it gave, and how long they took. With enough deals the same records fit the two judgment numbers that move its advice most: how hard pricing above value cuts the chance of a sale, and how much each quality factor is worth. Deals are kept in this browser; export them to keep a copy or move them.

    Build SDE from the financials

    Enter up to three years from the tax returns or income statements, most recent first; a blank counts as zero, and a figure in parentheses is a negative. Expense lines (pay, payroll taxes, perks, depreciation, interest, income taxes) are read as amounts spent and added back, and a “Less” line always deducts. Seller’s discretionary earnings (SDE) is what one owner-operator takes out of the business: income before income taxes, plus one working owner’s pay and perks, depreciation, interest, income taxes deducted above that line and one-time or personal items, less income that will not continue. Buyers and lenders ask for documentation of every add-back.
